ety.text: Inherited from Middle English no, noo, na, a reduced form of none, noon, nan (“none, not any”) used before consonants (compare a to an), from Old English nān (“none, not any”), from Proto-West Germanic *nain, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz (“not any”, literally “not one”), equivalent to ne (“not”) + a. Piecewise doublet of none.

Inherited from Middle English no, na, from Old English nā, nō (“no, not, not ever, never”), from Proto-West Germanic *naiwō, from Proto-Germanic *naiwô (“never”), from *ne (“not”) + *aiwō (“ever”), equivalent to ne + aye. Cognate with Scots na (“no”), Saterland Frisian noa (“no”), West Frisian né (“no”), nea (“never”), Dutch nee (“no”), Low German nee (“no”), German nie (“never”), dialectal German nö (“no”), Danish nej (“no”), Swedish nej (“no”), Icelandic nei (“no”). Doublet of nay.

ex: no one

senses.d: Not any possibility or allowance of (something).
ex: No smoking. No parking.
There's no stopping her once she gets going.

senses.d: Not (a); not properly, not really; not fully.
ex: My mother's no fool.
Working nine to five every day is no life.

senses.d: Used before different, before comparatives with more and less, and idiomatically before other comparatives.
ex: It is a less physical kind of torture, but no less gruesome.
I can think of no more deserving cause.

senses.d: Used idiomatically before certain other adjectives.
ex: This thing is no good.
The teacher’s decision was no fair.
I just want to find out whether she's coming or no.
Can ye no help me?

senses.d: Not, does not, do not, etc.
ex: Ug no like veggie.

senses.d: Used to show disagreement, negation, denial, refusal, or prohibition.
ex: No, you are mistaken.
No, you may not watch television now.

senses.d: Used to express sadness or disappointment.
ex: "We lost." "No!"
I got the job! / No! Really? That's fantastic!

senses.d: Used to show agreement with a negative question.
ex: "Don’t you like milk?" "No." (i.e., "No, I don’t like milk.")

senses.d: Used together with an affirmative word or phrase to show agreement.
ex: No, totally.
No, yeah, that's exactly right.
Look Ma, no hands!

senses.d: A negating expression; an answer that shows disagreement, denial, refusal, or disapproval.
ex: Q: I'll answer any ten questions that call for a yes or a no.

senses.d: A vote not in favor, or opposing a proposition.
ex: The workers voted on whether to strike, and there were thirty yeses and two nos.
“Heaven knows why a woman ‘Noes’!” / Clarrie nodded glumly. “And why she ‘Yesses’ in the end.”

senses.d: To answer with “no”; to decline, reject.
ex: BUDGET DIRECTOR SMITH / The President yessed his report […] SENATOR McCARRAN / He noed the President’s report

ety.text: From Old French alcun, from Vulgar Latin *alicunus, from Latin aliquī + unus. Cognate with Italian alcuno, Spanish alguno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.

From Latin nē (“not”) + ipse (emphatic, literally “himself”) + ūnus (“one”), by surface analysis “not even one”. Cognate with Neapolitan nisciuno, Sardinian nisciunu, Friulian nissun, Ligurian nisciǜn, and Old French neisune. Compare Spanish ninguno and Romanian niciun.
Inherited from Old Spanish no, non, from Latin nōn (compare Catalan no, Galician non, French non, Italian no, Portuguese não, Romanian nu, Sicilian no/nun).

es:ninguno.gl: no; none; (no/not…) at all, whatsoever, in the slightest; any (negative)

ety.text: Inherited from Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Compare Old French neisune, Italian nessuno and nissuno (Tuscan), Neapolitan nisciuno, Friulian nissun, Dalmatian nenčoin, Istriot ningun, Romanian niciun, Portuguese nenhum, Catalan ningú. By surface analysis, ni + uno.
From Old Galician-Portuguese nin (h)ũu, earlier nen (h)ũu, from Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Displaced the collateral form ningũu. Compare Galician ningún, Spanish ninguno.
